title: Push, Unload, Trim: Marrow Reserve, 2,3-DPG and Neocytolysis
summary: Learn how 2,3-DPG lowers haemoglobin’s oxygen affinity, why iron supply caps how far the marrow can raise red cell output, and what neocytolysis proposes about losing the youngest red cells after descent from altitude or early in spaceflight.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 32 Hits 1 (maximum marrow output), 6 (2,3-DPG) and 11 (neocytolysis). Hit 1 is checked against the Hillman and Henderson 1969 abstract (full text is page images only) and Saito 2014: output ranges from 2× to 8× depending on iron supply, so the lesson adds that context (register flag rv-ch32-marrow-max-iron). Hit 1’s “doubles at Hct 0.35 and triples at Hct 0.25 within 1 week” comes from a textbook not read and stays pending. Hit 11’s “postflight astronauts” is qualified: Risso 2014 places neocytolysis in the first days of flight, with post-landing anaemia linked to plasma re-expansion (rv-ch32-neocytolysis-inflight); Mairbäurl 2018 calls the mechanism unclear and the post-altitude evidence weak (rv-ch32-neocytolysis-uncertain). The Number Vault table is not taught in full and is not mapped. NCBI Bookshelf (StatPearls) pages were blocked by a captcha and not read.

objectives: Explain how 2,3-DPG binds deoxyhaemoglobin and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve.
State how iron supply limits the marrow’s maximum red cell output.
Describe neocytolysis, the settings where it is proposed, and its open questions.

scenes.title: Three oxygen problems
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three people whose red cells must adapt. (1) A patient with ongoing blood loss, iron-replete, taking oral iron; a note asks “Why isn’t the marrow at maximum?”. (2) A climber after weeks at high altitude with raised haemoglobin. (3) The same climber days after returning to sea level, haemoglobin falling faster than expected. Question token: “Push, unload, trim: how does the body tune red cells?”

cues.text: Three people, three oxygen problems. A patient with ongoing blood loss takes oral iron, yet the marrow is not producing at its maximum. Why not?
A climber spends weeks at high altitude and builds extra haemoglobin.
Back at sea level, the climber’s haemoglobin falls faster than expected. How does the body push, unload, and trim its red cells?

props.label: Push, unload, trim: how are red cells tuned?

scenes.title: Unloading: 2,3-DPG
scenes.altText: Schematic: a haemoglobin tetramer (two α, two β chains) with a central cavity. Card 1: 2,3-DPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) is made inside red cells from the glycolytic pathway. Card 2: it binds deoxyhaemoglobin more strongly than oxyhaemoglobin, one site per tetramer, in the central cavity at the β–β interface; it stabilises the low-affinity T state. Card 3: lower oxygen affinity shifts the dissociation curve to the right, so more oxygen is released to tissues; levels rise in chronic hypoxia. Card 4: rare BPG mutase deficiency leaves too little 2,3-DPG, raising oxygen affinity and causing erythrocytosis.

cues.text: First lever: unloading. Red cells make 2,3-DPG, also called 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, from a side branch of glycolysis.
It binds deoxyhaemoglobin far better than oxyhaemoglobin: one molecule per tetramer, in the central cavity where the two beta chains meet. That holds haemoglobin in its low-affinity tense state.
Lower affinity means a right shift of the dissociation curve, so more oxygen is released in the tissues. Levels rise in chronic hypoxia.
The reverse shows what it does. In rare BPG mutase deficiency, too little 2,3-DPG is made, haemoglobin holds oxygen tightly, and erythrocytosis can result.

scenes.title: Pushing: how far can the marrow go?
scenes.altText: Schematic bar chart of marrow red cell production in sustained anaemia (Hillman and Henderson 1969): normal = 1×; iron from normal stores or oral iron supports only about 2–3× normal; iron from haemolysis, non-viable red cells or iron dextran infusion lets production rise acutely to about 4–8× normal. Card: storage iron cannot be mobilised fast enough for a sudden large demand, so iron supply falls behind and production is held back (“iron-restricted erythropoiesis”). EPO card: EPO rises quickly in hypoxia, reticulocytes are released early, and the reticulocyte count peaks after about a week at altitude.

cues.text: Second lever: production. In sustained anaemia, erythropoietin drives the marrow, but iron supply sets the ceiling. In classic phlebotomy studies, output ranged from about twice to eight times normal.

Iron from normal stores, or iron by mouth, supported only about two to three times normal. Iron from haemolysis, from destroyed red cells, or from intravenous iron dextran let output climb acutely to four to eight times normal.
Why? Storage iron cannot be mobilised fast enough for a sudden large demand. The iron supply lags, and production is held back. Hillman called this iron-restricted erythropoiesis.
At altitude, erythropoietin rises quickly, young reticulocytes are released early, and the reticulocyte count peaks after about a week.

scenes.title: Trimming: neocytolysis
scenes.altText: Card 1: neocytolysis = selective destruction of the youngest circulating red cells (neocytes), soon after they leave the marrow, proposed to bring a raised red cell mass back down; it is linked to falling EPO. Card 2, descent: polycythaemic highland residents travelling to sea level lost about 9% of red cell mass within 3–7 days, with a rapid EPO fall and raised bilirubin; this did not occur in three subjects given EPO. Card 3, spaceflight: in the first days of flight plasma volume falls, haematocrit rises, EPO falls and red cell mass drops 10–15%; after landing, plasma volume re-expands and haematocrit falls. Card 4, caution: mechanism unclear (EPO withdrawal, weaker antioxidant defence); evidence after altitude described as weak; probably minor after moderate-altitude training. Hook answers token.

cues.text: Third lever: trimming. Neocytolysis is the proposed selective destruction of the youngest red cells, soon after they leave the marrow, to bring a raised red cell mass back down. It is linked to falling erythropoietin.

After descent: highland residents travelling to sea level lost about nine percent of their red cell mass within three to seven days, with a rapid fall in erythropoietin and a rise in bilirubin. Three people given erythropoietin did not show this.

In spaceflight, it is placed in the first days of flight: plasma volume falls, haematocrit rises, erythropoietin drops, and red cell mass falls by ten to fifteen percent. After landing, plasma re-expands and haematocrit falls.
Caution: the mechanism is unclear, and one review calls the evidence after altitude weak. Hook answers: oral iron limits output, altitude pushes it up, and descent may trim the newest cells.

props.label: Oral iron caps output · altitude pushes · descent may trim

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “2,3-DPG increases haemoglobin’s oxygen affinity” (✓ it lowers affinity and shifts the curve right); “High EPO means the marrow will reach eight times normal” (✓ with stores or oral iron, output reaches only about 2–3× normal; 4–8× needs iron from haemolysis or intravenous iron); “Neocytolysis removes the oldest red cells” (✓ it targets the youngest cells, the neocytes).

cues.text: Trap one: 2,3-DPG increases oxygen affinity. No: it lowers affinity and shifts the curve to the right.
Trap two: high erythropoietin means the marrow will reach eight times normal. No: on stores or oral iron, output reaches only two to three times normal.
Trap three: neocytolysis removes the oldest red cells. No: it targets the youngest ones, the neocytes.

scenes.title: Three Ds
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Three Ds: DPG Drops affinity; iron Decides how far the marrow goes; Descent Destroys the newest.” Tokens: Drops = right shift · Decides = 2–3× vs 4–8× · Destroys = neocytes. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: three Ds. 2,3-DPG drops oxygen affinity. Iron decides how far the marrow can go. Descent destroys the newest red cells.
Where it breaks: acid, carbon dioxide and heat also shift the curve right; neocytolysis is a hypothesis with an unclear mechanism; and in spaceflight it is placed early in flight, not after landing.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: H⁺, CO₂ and heat also shift right
Spaceflight: early in flight, not after landing

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “2,3-DPG binds deoxy-Hb at the β–β cavity → right shift”, “Marrow output ≈ 2–3× on stores or oral iron, up to ≈ 8× with haemolysis or IV iron”, “Neocytolysis: youngest red cells removed as EPO falls (proposed)”.

cues.text: 2,3-DPG lowers haemoglobin’s oxygen affinity, iron supply decides whether the marrow reaches two to three or up to eight times normal output, and neocytolysis is the proposed removal of the youngest red cells when erythropoietin falls.

props.label: Output ≈ 2–3× on stores/oral iron · up to ≈ 8× with haemolysis or IV iron
Neocytolysis: youngest cells removed as EPO falls (proposed)

explanation.what: Plain language: the body tunes red cells three ways. It helps haemoglobin let go of oxygen (2,3-DPG), it speeds up the marrow (erythropoietin, limited by iron), and it may remove the newest red cells when the extra ones are no longer needed (neocytolysis). Scientific terms: 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate), deoxyhaemoglobin, T state, oxygen dissociation curve, right shift, BPG mutase deficiency, erythropoietin (EPO), iron-restricted erythropoiesis, iron dextran, neocytes, neocytolysis, plasma volume.
explanation.why: 2,3-DPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhaemoglobin at the β–β interface and stabilises the low-affinity state, so more oxygen is unloaded. Marrow output depends on how fast iron can be delivered: storage iron cannot be mobilised fast enough for a large sudden demand. Neocytolysis is proposed to trim a red cell mass that has become larger than needed once the EPO stimulus falls.
explanation.measure: 2,3-DPG: binds deoxy-Hb, one site per tetramer; levels rise in chronic hypoxia; deficiency raises O₂ affinity. Marrow: about 2–3× normal on stores or oral iron; about 4–8× acutely with iron from haemolysis or iron dextran infusion. Neocytolysis: about 9% loss of red cell mass within 3–7 days after descent in highland residents; red cell mass falls 10–15% early in spaceflight.
explanation.differs: Right shift (more unloading: raised 2,3-DPG) vs left shift (tighter binding: 2,3-DPG deficiency); iron-limited 2–3× vs iron-rich 4–8× output; neocytolysis (youngest cells, linked to falling EPO) vs normal senescent removal (oldest cells, about 120 days).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the direction of the 2,3-DPG effect, why an iron-replete patient on oral iron does not reach maximal output, or which red cells neocytolysis removes and when.

comparisons.distinguisher: How fast iron reaches the marrow.

comparisons.title: Neocytolysis vs normal red cell removal
comparisons.distinguisher: Age of the cells removed and the trigger.

The 2–3× and 4–8× figures come from classic phlebotomy studies; individual responses vary.
takeaway: 2,3-DPG lowers haemoglobin’s oxygen affinity, iron supply decides whether the marrow reaches two to three or up to eight times normal output, and neocytolysis is the proposed removal of the youngest red cells when erythropoietin falls.

questions.stem: How does a rise in red cell 2,3-DPG affect oxygen delivery?

options.text: It binds deoxyhaemoglobin, lowers oxygen affinity and shifts the curve right, releasing more oxygen to tissues
options.rationale: Correct. 2,3-DPG stabilises the low-affinity deoxy (T) state, so more oxygen is unloaded.

options.text: It binds oxyhaemoglobin and shifts the curve left
options.rationale: Incorrect. It binds deoxyhaemoglobin far better than oxyhaemoglobin, and the shift is to the right.

options.text: It binds the α-chain heme iron and blocks oxygen binding
options.rationale: Incorrect. It binds the central cavity at the β–β interface, not the heme iron.

options.text: It has no effect on affinity; it only increases red cell count
options.rationale: Incorrect. Its main action is on affinity; 2,3-DPG deficiency raises affinity and can cause erythrocytosis.

questions.stem: An iron-replete patient with sustained blood loss is treated with oral iron. In classic phlebotomy studies, about how much could marrow red cell production rise under these conditions?

options.rationale: Correct. Iron from normal stores or oral iron supported only about 2–3× normal output.
Incorrect. Outputs of 4–8× were reached only when iron came from haemolysis, non-viable red cells or iron dextran infusion.

options.text: No rise until iron stores are empty
options.rationale: Incorrect. Output does rise, but storage iron cannot be mobilised fast enough for maximal output.
Incorrect. The classic studies reported a range of about 2× to 8× normal.

options.text: Proposed selective destruction of the youngest red cells, linked to falling erythropoietin, after descent from altitude or early in spaceflight
options.rationale: Correct. It targets neocytes and is linked to falling EPO; the mechanism is still unclear.

options.text: Removal of the oldest, senescent red cells at about 120 days
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is normal senescent removal, not neocytolysis.

options.text: Lysis of red cells caused by high 2,3-DPG
options.rationale: Incorrect. 2,3-DPG changes oxygen affinity; it is not the proposed trigger.

options.text: Destruction of red cells that is made worse by giving erythropoietin
options.rationale: Incorrect. In descending highlanders, the loss did not occur in three subjects given EPO.

claims.text: 2,3-DPG made via glycolysis; binds deoxy-Hb (one site, β–β central cavity); stabilises T state; right shift; rises in chronic hypoxia; BPG mutase deficiency causes high affinity and erythrocytosis.
Acid, CO₂ and heat also shift the curve right.
Marrow output 2× to 8× normal depending on iron supply; stores/oral iron 2–3×; haemolysis or iron dextran 4–8×; storage iron mobilised too slowly (iron-restricted erythropoiesis).
claims.note: Hillman 1969 checked from the abstract only.

claims.text: EPO rises quickly in hypoxia; early reticulocyte release; reticulocytes peak after about a week at altitude.
Neocytolysis definition; link to falling EPO; descent data; early-spaceflight data; plasma re-expansion after landing.
Reviewer: an iron-replete person doubles output within 1 week at Hct 0.35 and triples at Hct 0.25.
claims.note: Textbook source (Hillman and Finch) not read; not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 32 Hit 1 states that normal marrow can raise red cell production 6–8× normal under extreme stimulation. Hillman and Henderson 1969 (abstract) report 2× to 8× depending on iron supply: only about 2–3× with iron from stores or oral iron, and 4–8× only with iron from haemolysis, non-viable red cells or iron dextran; the lesson teaches the iron dependence (register flag rv-ch32-marrow-max-iron).

Ch. 32 Hit 11 places neocytolysis in “postflight astronauts”. Risso 2014 describes it during the first days of spaceflight, when plasma volume falls and EPO drops, and attributes the post-landing fall in haematocrit to plasma re-expansion; the lesson teaches the in-flight timing (register flag rv-ch32-neocytolysis-inflight).

Ch. 32 Hit 11 presents neocytolysis after EPO withdrawal as settled. Mairbäurl 2018 calls the mechanisms unclear (EPO withdrawal is supported by data on three subjects; impaired antioxidant capacity is an alternative) and the evidence after descent from altitude weak; Risso 2014 calls it a hypothesis (register flag rv-ch32-neocytolysis-uncertain).
